item.title: University of Stuttgart Deploys Quantum Dot QKD Link Using Frequency Conversion Over Campus Fiber
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article marks the first real‑world deployment of an entanglement‑based QKD link that relies on a quantum‑dot photon source combined with frequency conversion, showing that semiconductor emitters can now deliver metropolitan‑scale secure keys at practical rates. By generating 14.2 Mbit of key material over just 1.6 km of campus fiber and using it for one‑time‑pad image encryption, the work bridges laboratory demonstrations and operational quantum‑secure networks, complementing recent advances in fiber‑based QKD with atomic or nonlinear sources. The result suggests that compact, electrically driven quantum‑dot devices could become a cost‑effective backbone for future city‑wide cryptographic infrastructure, though scaling to longer distances will still require further loss mitigation and integration with existing telecom hardware.

The University of Stuttgart, in collaboration with Saarland University and Leibniz IFW Dresden, successfully deployed an entanglement-based quantum key distribution (QKD) link using a quantum dot photon source. The system generated 14.2 Mbit of secure key material over a 1.59 km fiber link, achieving one-time pad image encryption. This demonstrates the viability of quantum dots with frequency conversion for metropolitan quantum key networks. item.description:
Curator's Take: This article matters because microwave crosstalk has long limited the scalability of superconducting qubit arrays, and Chalmers’ parasitic‑capacitance engineering offers a hardware‑level fix that does not rely on additional control circuitry. By deliberately shaping on‑chip capacitances to create destructive interference, the team aligns classical crosstalk nulls with quantum ZZ interaction nulls—a synergy that complements recent advances in floating transmon designs and error‑mitigation protocols. If the approach proves robust across larger chips, it could simplify wiring layouts and reduce calibration overhead for near‑term processors, though its effectiveness will need validation on multi‑qubit devices beyond the demonstrated prototypes.

Physicists at Chalmers University of Technology have developed a new method to eliminate microwave crosstalk in superconducting processors. Their research shows that by engineering on-chip parasitic capacitances, they can achieve destructive interference among parasitic capacitive channels, suppressing unwanted qubit excitations. This method offers a practical advantage for floating transmons and allows for alignment of classical microwave crosstalk nulls with quantum ZZ nulls. item.title: Los Alamos and QC Ware Model Correlated Iron Oxides Using Sample-Based Quantum Diagonalization on IBM Hardware
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that a hybrid quantum‑classical workflow can finally reach chemical accuracy on notoriously difficult strongly correlated iron oxides, a class of materials that have long frustrated conventional electronic‑structure methods. By deploying Sample‑based Quantum Diagonalization on IBM’s superconducting processors and feeding it tight‑binding models derived from ab initio data, the Los Alamos–QC Ware team not only reproduced experimental ground states for FeO and Fe₂O₂ but also outperformed state‑of‑the‑art classical approaches, hinting at a scalable path toward bulk periodic simulations. The result demonstrates that near‑term quantum hardware can already add tangible value to materials science, though further improvements in qubit fidelity and error mitigation will be needed before routine industrial deployment.

Researchers from Los Alamos National Laboratory and QC Ware developed a hybrid quantum-classical workflow to simulate strongly correlated transition metal oxides. They used Sample-based Quantum Diagonalization (SQD) on IBM Quantum hardware, coupled with ab initio-informed d–p tight-binding models, to achieve chemical accuracy in modeling diatomic iron monoxide (FeO) and rhombic iron oxide dimers (Fe2O2). This method successfully recovered experimental ground states and outperformed traditional computational methods, establishing a new approach for modeling bulk periodic FeO. item.title: Sandia and Quantinuum Introduce Logical Gate Set Tomography to Map Fault-Tolerant Qubit Noise
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article reports the first self‑consistent tomographic reconstruction of an entire universal single‑qubit logical gate set—“Logical GST”—demonstrated on a Steane‑code logical qubit in Quantinuum’s H1‑1 processor. By confirming that error correction largely reduces physical noise to simple Pauli‑stochastic channels while also exposing subtle coherent over‑rotations and non‑Markovian effects, the work provides a crucial diagnostic tool for tightening fault‑tolerance thresholds as hardware scales. The ability to map logical‑level errors directly will help both academia and industry refine control strategies and benchmark next‑generation error‑corrected processors.

Researchers from Sandia National Laboratories and Quantinuum have introduced "Logical GST," a protocol that provides the first self-consistent, full tomographic reconstruction of a universal single-qubit logical gate set. This was implemented on a single logical qubit encoded in the [[7, 1, 3]] Steane code on the Quantinuum System Model H1-1. The study confirmed the assumption that quantum error correction converts complex physical noise into simple, uncorrelated Pauli-stochastic channels, but high-shot emulation revealed small but statistically significant logical non-Markovianity and coherent logical over-rotations. item.title: Weighted hypergraph states as a resource for quantum metrology
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that weighted hypergraph states—an extension of familiar graph‑state entanglement—can be engineered to give a genuine metrological edge even when the underlying controlled interactions are weak and subject to dephasing. By deriving closed‑form quantum Fisher information for arbitrary N and demonstrating that higher‑order hyperedges boost both precision scaling and noise tolerance, the work bridges a gap between abstract multipartite entanglement theory and realistic sensor hardware. It builds on recent efforts to find practical, robust entangled probes beyond fragile GHZ or Dicke states, suggesting a new design space for quantum‑enhanced magnetometers, clocks, and interferometers that can operate under realistic noise levels.

Quantum correlations can be used to improve sensing precision beyond classical limits, yet the correlated resource states needed can be challenging to prepare and preserve. Here, we study the family of weighted hypergraph states and identify subclasses characterized by their underlying graph topology that exhibit enhanced metrological performance. Using the quantum Fisher information and a novel Dicke state basis representation, we show that these subclasses outperform both separable and standard weighted graph state benchmarks over broad ranges of edge weights corresponding to weak controlled operations between qubits representing the vertices of the graph. We provide analytical formulas for an arbitrary number $N$ of qubits, supplemented by a general study, while focusing a detailed analysis on the example case of $N=4$. By identifying the critical probabilities for local dephasing, we show that adding higher-order weighted hyperedges for $N$ qubits can enhance metrological robustness, allowing the resulting states to retain a quantum advantage at higher noise levels. These probe states exhibit favorable scaling, enhanced precision, and noise tolerance. Our findings establish weighted hypergraph states as viable, structurally tunable and robust resources for quantum-enhanced metrology.

item.title: Topologically Protected Edge States in a Single Flux Qubit
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates that a single inductively shunted flux qubit can host topologically protected edge states, showing that the exotic protection mechanisms usually associated with large‑scale lattice models are attainable in a minimal superconducting circuit. By mapping the device onto an extended Su–Schrieffer–Heeger chain and confirming the behavior numerically, the authors bridge condensed‑matter concepts of graphene‑like honeycomb potentials with practical qubit engineering, suggesting a new route to mitigate charge‑noise decoherence without scaling up to multi‑qubit arrays. If experimentally realized, such intrinsic topological protection could simplify hardware designs for robust quantum processors, though the protection hinges on preserving chiral symmetry, so real‑world imperfections that break this symmetry will still need careful management.

We show that topological edge states can be realized in a simple superconducting circuit composed of an inductively shunted flux qubit. The Josephson potential of that qubit forms a honeycomb lattice similar to the case of graphene. The additional shunting element produces a quartic potential along one flux direction, which effectively creates a boundary in flux space. We map analytically the low-energy dynamics of the circuit to an extended Su--Schrieffer--Heeger (SSH) chain, in which a quartic potential is added to the usual SSH Hamiltonian. This mapping is confirmed by numerical simulations of the full superconducting circuit. We argue that chiral symmetry still holds for the edge states of the extended model around a chiral point in parameter space. Close to this point, we numerically find that edge states in our superconducting circuit are topologically protected against perturbations that obey chiral symmetry, as is the case for charge noise. Our results show that topological effects previously thought to occur in multi-qubit systems, such as protection against decoherence, can also be found in much simpler single superconducting qubits.

item.title: Benchmarking Single-Photon Sources for Measurement-Device-Independent Quantum Key Distribution
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article matters because it provides the first systematic benchmark showing that quantum‑dot single‑photon emitters can outpace even optimally tuned weak‑coherent pulse sources across all realistic fiber distances in measurement‑device‑independent QKD. By integrating decoy‑state analysis and realistic Hong‑Ou‑Mandel visibility constraints, the authors demonstrate how sub‑Poissonian statistics translate into higher key rates and longer reach—key steps toward scalable, hardware‑secure quantum networks. The work also highlights that both source families remain extremely vulnerable to imperfect photon indistinguishability, underscoring the need for continued advances in emitter purity and interferometric stability.

Measurement-Device-Independent Quantum Key Distribution (MDI-QKD) enables secure communication without trusting the measurement devices, but its performance critically depends on the quality of the employed photon sources. We compare MDI-QKD implementations based on Weak Coherent Pulses (WCPs) with those employing Quantum Dot (QD) single-photon sources. WCP-based schemes are fundamentally limited by Poissonian photon-number statistics, imposing a trade-off between single- and multi-photon emissions, whereas QD sources exhibit sub-Poissonian statistics with low antibunching parameter $g^{(2)}(0)$. Using a decoy-state analysis for both source types, we find that even at moderate mean photon numbers, QD-based implementations outperform the best-case WCP configuration - where the mean photon number is optimised at each transmission distance - across the full range of transmission distances. We further incorporate the effect of imperfect photon indistinguishability via Hong-Ou-Mandel interference visibilities into the security framework and demonstrate that both source types are highly sensitive to even small deviations from ideal indistinguishability, significantly affecting achievable key rates and maximum transmission distance.

item.title: Empirical Evaluation of Quantum Kernel Methods for Classification: A Comparative Study with Classical Kernels
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that once measurement budgets, hyper‑parameter tuning and evaluation costs are rigorously controlled, quantum kernel classifiers offer no statistically significant accuracy boost over a well‑tuned classical RBF kernel on real‑world datasets. By treating the comparison itself as an experimental variable, the authors reveal that most of the observed performance gain comes from bandwidth tuning rather than any intrinsic quantum advantage, calling into question earlier benchmark claims that omitted these controls. The work underscores that near‑term quantum machine‑learning research must prioritize fair protocol design and hardware improvements before expecting practical superiority over classical methods.

Quantum kernel methods are the most concrete near-term proposal for quantum machine learning on classical data, yet published benchmarks disagree on whether they outperform tuned classical kernels, and the disagreement cannot be resolved from the literature because the comparisons are not protocol-controlled. We argue that the obstacle is one of measurement, not theory: the usual setup fixes the quantum feature map's data scaling while grid-searching the classical kernel's hyperparameters, recomputes nothing per fold, and reports cost in simulator time. We therefore treat the comparison itself as the object of study and impose three controls. The bandwidth is tuned on the same grid budget as the classical $γ$, the kernel is recomputed inside every fold from fold-fitted preprocessing, and cost is counted in hardware circuit evaluations. On top of these we run a factorial design of 324 cells in which dimensionality, training size, class separability and data structure are explicit covariates, together with four standard datasets, a shots-versus-gate-noise ablation, and a cost sweep. The dominant effect we measure is not quantum: tuning the feature map's bandwidth is worth 0.120 accuracy on synthetic data and 0.339 on real data, exceeding every quantum-classical difference we observe. Tuned quantum kernels are then statistically indistinguishable from a tuned RBF on all four real datasets. The advantage on synthetic data is confined almost entirely to data generated by the feature map itself, and it shrinks with dimensionality (-0.0045 per qubit) while growing with sample size. Finite sampling costs an order of magnitude more accuracy than gate and readout noise, and a fidelity kernel needs $5\times10^{7}$ circuits at n = 10,000. Protocol variance is thus sufficient to explain the field's contradictory conclusions.

item.title: Resource efficient Sample Based Quantum Simulation through Fragmentation and Virtual Partitioning of QPU
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates a practical route to scaling quantum‑chemical simulations on today’s noisy devices by fragmenting the problem and virtually partitioning the QPU, cutting two‑qubit depth by up to half and slashing runtime by more than 80 % while still reaching chemical accuracy. By coupling a “half‑qubit” ansatz with an HCI expansion, the authors show that only a vanishing fraction of the determinant space needs to be sampled, enabling active spaces as large as 104 spin orbitals on 52 qubits—far beyond what prior sample‑based methods could handle. The work directly tackles the twin bottlenecks of circuit depth and classical post‑processing in quantum‑centric supercomputing, suggesting that near‑term hardware can now address chemically relevant systems such as drug‑target complexes.

Present-day sample-based quantum algorithms within quantum-centric supercomputing workflows require substantial classical post-processing, large circuit depths to produce chemically relevant samples, and long QPU times to execute the many circuits needed for molecules of chemically relevant size. We introduce FMO-QVM-HCI-HSQD, a resource-efficient sample-based framework that breaks a large problem into fragments, runs the fragments in parallel on virtual regions of the QPU, and reduces circuit depth through a half-qubit ansatz whose samples seed an HCI expansion. We demonstrate the algorithm on ibm_marrakesh and ibm_boston for the water trimer and the carmofur_Mpro complex with up to 52 qubits, benchmarking against FMO-CCSD(T), FMO-CASCI and FMO-HCI. For the water trimer (14 spin orbitals for monomers, 28 for dimers), our method reduces the two-qubit depth by 39% compared to FMO-QVM-SQD and the QPU time by 82% compared to sequential FMO-SQD, and accesses 3% of the determinant subspace versus 40% for FMO-SQD, while achieving more accurate energies. For the carmofur_Mpro complex (16 and 32 spin orbitals), it reduces the two-qubit depth by 47% and the QPU time by 20% compared to FMO-QVM-SQD, and accesses 0.007% of the determinant subspace versus 40%, while remaining within chemical accuracy. Extending the carmofur_Mpro active space in the 6-31G basis to 52 and 104 spin orbitals, sampled on 26 and 52 qubits, the total energy deviates from FMO-HCI by only 1.22 mHa. These results show that combining fragmentation, virtual QPU partitioning and half-qubit sampling makes sample-based quantum simulation of chemically relevant systems feasible on current hardware.

item.title: Control-Noise Trade-offs in Industrially Integrated ${}^{28}\mathrm{Si}/\mathrm{SiGe}$ Spin-1/2 Qubits
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that silicon‑spin qubits fabricated in a commercial 300 mm foundry can already achieve primitive gate fidelities of 99.99 % while displaying improved idle coherence and reduced device‑to‑device variability, demonstrating that industrial processes are no longer a barrier to high‑quality quantum hardware. The work also reveals a subtle control‑noise trade‑off: moving micromagnets farther from the quantum well—necessary for back‑end‑of‑line routing in dense two‑dimensional arrays— lowers magnetic gradients, which suppresses charge‑noise‑induced frequency jitter but weakens electrically driven spin resonance and makes drive errors more prominent at modest Rabi rates. These findings give foundries concrete design knobs to balance scalability with control performance as silicon spin qubits move toward fault‑tolerant architectures.

Scaling silicon spin qubits to fault-tolerant processors requires semiconductor foundry integration, yet it remains unclear how industrial fabrication and dense device integration affect qubit control and noise. Here we study ${}^{28}\mathrm{Si}/\mathrm{SiGe}$ electron spin-1/2 qubits fabricated using Intel's industry-compatible 300 mm process and incorporating micromagnets for electrically driven spin resonance, using a high-performance device fabricated in the RIKEN research cleanroom as a reference. Primitive $π/2$-gate fidelities reach the 99.99% level in the Intel devices, which also exhibit longer idle coherence, weaker low-frequency correlations and reduced qubit-to-qubit variability across several measured characteristics. In the present Intel devices, the micromagnets are integrated inline with the back-end-of-line (BEOL) contact routing, with their separation from the quantum well set through the vertical stack design. Relative to the reference, their larger separation contributes to weaker longitudinal and transverse magnetic-field gradients. The weaker longitudinal gradient suppresses the conversion of charge noise into qubit-frequency fluctuations, whereas the weaker transverse gradient reduces electrically driven spin-resonance efficiency and makes drive-dependent errors relevant at lower Rabi frequencies. Additional BEOL routing and metal levels required for two-dimensional arrays make such placement decisions increasingly consequential when scaling. item.title: Hybrid Quantum Algorithms for Trade Surveillance Analytics
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that hybrid quantum‑classical classifiers can already rival most conventional machine‑learning models on a realistic anti‑money‑laundering task, with the HQNN beating six of eight classical baselines and delivering competitive F1 scores even on noisy IBM hardware. By combining a tiny five‑qubit circuit with a classical network that sets every rotation angle, the authors demonstrate a practical route to leverage near‑term quantum devices for high‑dimensional financial analytics—a field where recent advances in quantum kernels and QNNs have struggled to scale. Although XGBoost still leads, the results suggest that hybrid approaches could soon narrow the gap between quantum prototypes and production‑grade fraud detection systems.

Anti-money laundering (AML) and trade surveillance remain largely manual: rule-based monitoring raises alerts of which, by estimate, over 95% are false positives, each reviewed by a human analyst. We benchmark four quantum and hybrid classifiers against classical baselines on a synthetic pump-and-dump detection task: a fidelity-based quantum k-nearest-neighbours classifier (QKNN) with clustering-based routing; a quantum support vector machine (QSVM) on a one-body projected quantum kernel; a 20-qubit quantum neural network (QNN) with a Pauli-ZZ feature map and RealAmplitudes ansatz; and a hybrid quantum neural network (HQNN) in which a small classical network generates every rotation angle of a five-qubit circuit. Baselines are logistic regression, XGBoost, one- and three-hidden-layer neural networks, and classical k-nearest neighbours. All models share one stratified split of 1000 accounts (800 train, 200 test, 20% suspicious) and two 20-feature representations (ANOVA and PCA); QKNN and QSVM are also tested under simulated noise, and the HQNN is run on the ibm_fez processor. The best model is classical XGBoost on ANOVA features, at a suspicious-class F1 of 61.4%. The HQNN is the strongest quantum-hybrid model, at 54.5-57.9% F1 on an ideal simulator and 55.4-59.8% on ibm_fez, ahead of six of eight classical configurations; at a 15% false-positive rate, half its alerts are genuinely suspicious. Versus the QNN (42.0% F1), it raises under half the false alarms at similar recall with a quarter of the qubits. The QKNN reaches 43.5% F1 (44.4% under noise), above classical KNN (35.6%); the QSVM does not exceed 41%. We observe no quantum advantage, but a five-qubit hybrid on today's noisy hardware already matches well-tuned classical models, with room to grow via richer circuits and larger devices. We contribute a like-for-like comparison with classical models on shared data, splits and features.

In this work, we demonstrate a significant performance gap using a projected quantum kernel for $n=15,30$ and $45$ qubits over classical methods on an engineered classification problem, and show reproducibility of the results over different quantum processor units. item.title: Overcoming the Representational Limitations of Amplitude Encoding for Quantum Neural Networks
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article pinpoints a fundamental blind spot in amplitude‑encoded quantum neural networks: the unavoidable loss of information under uniform real scaling, which caps their expressive power regardless of circuit depth. By introducing a simple, parameter‑free nonlinear preprocessing step that restores sensitivity to all real inputs while preserving the logarithmic qubit advantage, the authors deliver a practical encoding upgrade that boosts benchmark classification accuracy by 21–44 % over both standard amplitude and angle encodings. The result is a timely advance for near‑term QNN implementations, showing that smarter data preparation can extract far more performance from limited quantum hardware without adding trainable complexity.

Quantum Neural Networks (QNNs) offer a framework for learning functions from classical data, but their expressive power depends critically on how inputs are encoded into quantum states. Angle encoding can require resources that scale with the number of features, whereas amplitude encoding represents $d$ features using only $\mathcal{O}(\log_2 d)$ qubits. This compactness comes at a representational cost: normalization makes conventional amplitude encoding invariant to nonzero real rescaling of the input, up to an unobservable global phase. We show that this invariance induces an exact, architecture-independent restriction on the resulting hypothesis class. No downstream quantum circuit can distinguish inputs differing by nonzero real scaling. We develop a general condition under which deterministic preprocessing can remove this ambiguity and show that nonlinearity alone is insufficient. Based on this analysis, we introduce a fixed nonlinear feature map that provably distinguishes all real inputs under subsequent amplitude encoding, without adding trainable parameters and while retaining logarithmic qubit scaling. We evaluate the resulting QNN on three canonical classification benchmarks and a nonlinear synthetic dataset against conventional amplitude and angle encoding, as well as a classical neural network. Across these tasks, the proposed encoding consistently improves classification accuracy over both quantum encoding baselines by 21$-$44 %. Our results establish normalization-induced scale invariance as a concrete representational bottleneck of amplitude encoding and demonstrate that it can be removed while preserving a compact quantum representation, marking a step toward quantum models capable of capturing arbitrary relationships in classical data.

item.title: Bounding Fidelity of Non-Stabilizer States from Local Pauli Measurements
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article tackles a long‑standing bottleneck in quantum verification by showing how the “magic” needed for universal computation can be certified with only linear‑scaling Pauli measurements, sidestepping the exponential blow‑up that plagues direct fidelity estimation of non‑stabilizer states. By exploiting permutational symmetry and casting the problem as a small linear program, the authors demonstrate practical protocols that remain tractable even for hundreds of qubits—a scale relevant to near‑term quantum processors and distributed quantum networks. The approach not only cuts measurement overhead but also opens the door to efficiently monitoring other nonlinear resources such as purity, although its performance still depends on how well the assumed symmetries match real hardware noise.

Nonstabilizerness, commonly referred to as magic, is essential for universal quantum computation. Yet, for pure $n$-qubit states this property is directly linked to the hardness of direct fidelity estimation. We propose a scheme to bound the fidelity on non-stabilizer states by choosing operators with low measurement overhead and using parallel local Pauli measurements to estimate compatible observables. We selectively measure operators that share a permutational symmetry without imposing any assumption on the physical system. This selection reduces the optimization to a linear program with only $O(n)$ variables for bounding fidelity. Our methods can be extended to bound nonlinear quantities like the purity via convex quadratic programs. For hypergraph states that can exhibit extensive nonstabilizerness, we demonstrate for up to $n=500$ qubits that our framework substantially reduces the measurement overhead under both local and global depolarizing noise. These results show that symmetry induced by measurement selection reduces both measurement and computational costs, enabling scalable characterization of magic resources in quantum computing and quantum networks.

item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that a smart, adaptive choice of scalarisation weights can dramatically cut the number of noisy QAOA runs needed to map out Pareto fronts in multi‑objective materials design, turning query efficiency into a near‑term advantage for NISQ hardware. By framing weight selection as Bayesian optimisation and using expected hypervolume improvement, BW‑QAMOO achieves up to a 74 % reduction in solves compared with naïve uniform sampling, especially as the number of objectives grows. Materials design is a multi-objective problem, and recent advances in quantum optimization make it possible to bring quantum solvers to bear on such problems. The realistic near-term win, though, is not raw quantum advantage but making an expensive, noisy quantum solver usable by spending its calls wisely. Quantum Approximate Multi-Objective Optimization (QAMOO) traces a Pareto front by solving a family of scalarized Ising problems, one per objective-weight vector, with QAOA --- but chooses those weights \emph{non-adaptively}, sampling them at random, blind to what it has already found. On a frustrated alloy-configuration benchmark across $m\in\{3,4\}$ objectives and $n\in\{10,11,12\}$ sites, BW-QAMOO reaches the same Pareto hypervolume as QAMOO's random sampling with a median 33% fewer scalarized solves across the 90/95\% targets and 60--74\% fewer than a uniform-grid baseline), on a genuine (simulated) QAOA solver; a paired Wilcoxon test confirms the saving is significant, and the advantage grows with the objective count m as the weight simplex expands and blind sampling wastes more of the budget. This is a \emph{query-efficiency} result, and we close with the open challenges on the path to real alloy data and hardware.

item.title: Leveraging Quantum Measurement Randomness for Shot-Efficient Diffusion Models
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows how the inevitable shot noise of quantum readout can be turned into a feature rather than a bug, letting a diffusion‑based quantum generative model replace part of its injected randomness with the hardware’s own measurement fluctuations. By analytically matching the mean and covariance of the ideal update, the authors derive an adaptive shot budget that cuts required measurements from millions to just a few hundred while preserving sample quality on Gaussian mixtures and MNIST latent spaces. The result tackles one of the biggest practical hurdles for quantum neural networks—expensive repeated sampling—and could bring near‑term quantum generative AI within reach, though scaling beyond low‑dimensional demos remains an open challenge.

In quantum computing, the readout always carries finite-shot sampling noise. Suppressing this noise through repeated measurements raises the cost of a quantum neural network (QNN). Meanwhile, a stochastic diffusion sampler deliberately adds randomness at each reverse (generation) step. This paper turns the measurement noise from a liability into a resource. Specifically, we use the noise quantum measurement produces anyway to replace part of the noise the sampler would otherwise inject. We characterize the measurement error as multinomial sampling noise propagated through a trainable linear readout. To connect the circuit's Born probabilities to the denoising task, we further formulate the diffusion process on a bounded zero-sum hyperplane mapped to the probability simplex. Therefore, we can employ a compensation noise to match the mean and covariance of the shot-noise-free linear update under some minimum shot conditions. Solving this condition for the shot count gives a state-dependent adaptive budget. For the denoising diffusion implicit model (DDIM), this budget increases as the sampler becomes more deterministic. On an eight-dimensional Gaussian mixture, the schedule achieves comparable generation quality with $303$ shots per sample against a high-shot reference of $1.6\times10^{6}$, about $5300\times$ fewer. Latent diffusion experiments on MNIST further validate the proposed mechanism for generation in a learned latent space.

item.title: A Highly Nondegenerate Photon-Pair Source for Detector-Matched Quantum Key Distribution
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates a clever way to cut the dominant hardware expense in entanglement‑based QKD by generating highly nondegenerate photon pairs so that only the telecom‑wavelength photon needs an expensive cryogenic detector while the visible partner can be caught with a cheap, high‑efficiency Si‑SPAD. By showing that even an unoptimised source already narrows the cost per secret bit to within 25 % of a conventional dual‑SNSPD link—and that realistic improvements could slash total expense by up to 70 %—the work points toward more economically scalable quantum‑secure networks. The result dovetails with current industry pushes for integrated, low‑cost photonic sources and highlights that the remaining challenge is boosting collection efficiency and brightness before large‑scale deployment.

In a commercial entanglement-distribution system over telecom fibre, the single-photon detectors are the largest part of the hardware cost. In entanglement-based quantum key distribution (QKD), both photons of each pair must be detected. With two telecom photons, each arm needs either an InGaAs single-photon avalanche diode (SPAD) of low efficiency or a superconducting nanowire single-photon detector (SNSPD) with its own cryostat. We study a highly nondegenerate photon-pair source that needs a telecom detector on one arm only. Two periodically poled KTiOPO$_4$ (ppKTP) crystals pumped at 405~nm emit pairs at 548 and 1550~nm. A Si-SPAD with 82\% efficiency detects the 548~nm photon at the source node, and only the 1550~nm photon travels through fibre. A first, unoptimised module in a polarisation-correlated configuration generates about $1.5\times10^6$ pairs/s per mW of pump power. It collects 13\% of the pairs on the 548~nm arm and 23\% on the 1550~nm arm. In an asymptotic BBM92 model, we compare its links with generic $2\times1550$~nm links that use a bright published source at the same pump power. At 50~km, our link with one SNSPD costs about 25\% more per secret bit than the generic link with one SNSPD. With optimistic target values of 52\% collection and twice the brightness, it costs about 40\% as much as the generic link with two SNSPDs. Our link without a cryostat then costs about 70\% less than the generic link with one SNSPD. If every link runs at its own best pump power, the two-SNSPD link is again the cheapest. The source can also serve clock synchronisation and detector calibration, which need only time-correlated pairs. All key rates assume the entangled configuration of the source, which is under development.

The corresponding cost Hamiltonian for MAX-$k$-CUT problem on hypergraphs is reduced to an Ising Hamiltonian with pairwise interactions. This reduction simplifies the solution of the MAX-$k$-CUT problem using quantum computing. As illustrative examples, a 3-uniform tight-star hypergraph and a sunflower hypergraph are considered. The corresponding Hamiltonians are constructed, and quantum protocols for the MAX-$k$-CUT problems are presented. The MAX-3-CUT and MAX-4-CUT instances are investigated for these hypergraphs by varying the number of Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) layers from (p=2) to (p=15) with quantum computing on IBM's Qiskit AerSimulator.

item.title: Mathematical foundations of second quantization: an introduction through spin-boson models
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article delivers a rare, mathematically rigorous bridge between the abstract machinery of second quantization and the concrete spin‑boson models that underlie many superconducting qubit architectures, showing exactly how ladder operators, Fock spaces and canonical commutation relations give rise to well‑posed Hamiltonians. By proving self‑adjointness, providing explicit spectra for Jaynes‑Cummings and Rabi‑type systems, and even delivering a quantified rotating‑wave approximation error bound, it equips hardware designers with trustworthy analytical tools for modeling decoherence and engineered dissipation. In an era where quantum processors are increasingly judged by their noise mitigation strategies, such solid foundations help translate theoretical insights into more reliable device simulations and error‑corrected control protocols.

These lecture notes originate from a one-semester course on the mathematical foundations of second quantization, first given at the Department of Physics of the Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg in the Winter Semester 2025/26 to a mixed audience of physics and mathematics students. Their guiding thread is a class of physical models: spin-boson models, describing a two-level system coupled to a boson field. After summarizing the necessary background on unbounded operators, up to the Kato-Rellich and KLMN theorems, and developing direct sums and tensor products of Hilbert spaces and of unbounded operators, we treat single-mode boson fields, constructing the ladder and number operators and characterizing their domains, before moving to Fock spaces, second quantization, bosonic and fermionic annihilation and creation operators, and the canonical (anti)commutation relations. Throughout, spin-boson models provide both the motivation and the test bench for the formalism: we rigorously establish their self-adjointness, solve the pure dephasing and Jaynes-Cummings models explicitly, deriving their spectra and the qubit channels they induce, show how their multimode counterparts display irreversible decoherence and decay, and, in an appendix, prove the rotating-wave approximation for the quantum Rabi model with an explicit error bound. Finally, we use the KLMN theorem to construct spin-boson models with non-normalizable form factors, and briefly discuss stronger ultraviolet divergences and the need for renormalization. Exercises with full solutions are included.

Quantum data reuploading models can increase the expressive capacity of variational quantum models, but do not necessarily improve predictive performance. In the present work, we investigate this behavior for seasonal time series forecasting and show that data encoding determines how well temporal structures are represented as circuit depth increases. We develop a fidelity-based quantum geometric description in which repeated encodings contribute to an effective input generator, so that reuploading depth changes the quantum geometry through which approximately recurrent inputs are distinguished. Noisy simulations show that this encoding hierarchy persists at shallow and intermediate depths, while larger depths are limited by circuit noise and optimization difficulty. The seasonal quantum models remain competitive with established classical forecasting methods (ARIMA, random forests, and LSTMs). These results identify structure-aware quantum data encoding as a general strategy for building deeper quantum reuploading models.

Curator's Take: This article delivers the first systematic low‑energy model for the newly demonstrated cos 2φ transmon, showing how engineered symmetries can be captured in a compact Born–Oppenheimer description that makes selection rules and noise protection transparent. Engineered symmetries in superconducting circuits can protect quantum information; much like selection rules in atomic physics, they forbid transitions between the qubit states. Protected circuits, however, combine several loops and islands and host multiple nonlinearly coupled modes, calling for reduced low-energy models that inherit the circuit symmetries and make the protection manifest. We develop such a reduction for the $\cos 2\varphi$ transmon qubit, recently realized experimentally with a two-Cooper-pair interferometer, whose circuit hosts three coupled modes. Exploiting the separation of energy scales between the heavy transmon mode and the light internal modes of the interferometer, we derive an effective single-band Born-Oppenheimer model, including its geometric correction, and extend it to several bands. We identify the symmetries of the full and reduced Hamiltonians and derive exact selection rules. Finally, we identify a parameter regime beyond the single-band description that suppresses flux-noise dephasing without degrading charge-noise protection.

We introduce FaultScope, a classical simulator for quantum error correction circuits, implemented in Rust with a Python interface. FaultScope estimates logical error rates and their derivatives with respect to component error rates from the same sampled and decoded shots, without modifying or differentiating through the decoder. These derivatives enable error attribution to individual noisy components, helping identify noise hotspots for targeted noise reduction. FaultScope supports forward simulation of error propagation through circuits and direct sampling of detector and logical observable outcomes from detector error models. In our noiseless and noisy benchmarks, FaultScope has the lowest runtime among the tested simulators at every size. Computing all derivatives adds only 0.33--0.97\% to the runtime of logical error rate estimation across five repetition code sizes with 7--2047 error locations. FaultScope can be used to benchmark large-scale quantum error correction schemes and guide targeted noise reduction efficiently, thereby facilitating the design and optimization of fault-tolerant quantum computing architectures.

item.title: High-efficiency photonic GHZ measurements with linear optics
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that by exploiting many‑body interference in linear‑optical circuits, photonic GHZ measurements can reach a success probability of 9/32 for four photons—far above the ~1/4 limit of conventional Bell‑fusion schemes—and that the method scales exponentially better for larger entangled states. The higher‑efficiency fusions directly translate into faster generation of graph‑state resources and more reliable entanglement distribution across spin‑photon interfaces, addressing a key bottleneck in fusion‑based quantum computing architectures. While still probabilistic and requiring adaptive post‑selection, the approach provides a practical new primitive that could shrink overheads for scalable photonic processors.

Probabilistic and destructive Bell-measurements, also known as fusions, constitute a fundamental primitive for photonic quantum technologies. These operations rely only on pairwise photonic interference, whereas the computational power of photonic quantum systems originates from many-body interference. Here, we introduce a family of high-efficiency linear-optical GHZ measurements based on four-mode interferometers and show that incorporating many-body interference into this ubiquitous primitive leads to more efficient entangling operations. For the four-photon case, the success probability is $9/32$, and adaptive variants ensure that unsuccessful events project onto useful stabilizer states. We further show that the approach naturally generalizes to larger GHZ measurements, yielding an exponentially higher success probability than previous linear-optical schemes. Finally, we demonstrate practical advantages for graph-state resource generation, entanglement distribution between remote spin-photon interfaces, and fusion-based quantum computing. item.title: eCAS: An Orbital Embedding Method for Quantum Computing
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article introduces eCAS, a new orbital‑embedding framework that sidesteps the costly reduced‑density‑matrix measurements and repeated circuit evaluations that have hampered most quantum‑embedding schemes to date. By partitioning the problem into independent localized active spaces via a Schmidt‑decomposed impurity–bath construction, eCAS can be tackled with any existing VQE or QPE algorithm, making it far more amenable to near‑term fault‑tolerant hardware. Its systematic “mutual correlation” criterion offers a clear path for incremental accuracy without iterative self‑consistency loops, positioning the method as a practical bridge between current quantum chemistry algorithms and the larger atomistic simulations envisioned for future quantum computers.

Future fault-tolerant quantum computers will allow us to calculate electronic structures of atomistic systems. However, these systems will be intrinsically limited in size, requiring embedding theories for many systems because of the unfavorable scaling of the number of terms describing the electron-electron interaction in the second-quantized electronic Hamiltonian. Quantum embedding theories address this challenge by partitioning a quantum system into a region of interest, the impurity, and its (larger) complement, the environment. However, currently available quantum embedding methods place restrictive demands on near-future quantum computers, such as the need to measure reduced density matrices or the need for repeated evaluations. Here, we introduce the new orbital embedding method eCAS that steers clear of these pitfalls by constructing a multi-CAS problem, the active spaces of which are localized and can be solved independently of each other with any quantum algorithm. This also allows for the development of comparatively simple gradient expressions. eCAS leverages the Schmidt decomposition to construct initial impurity and bath orbitals and augments them with localized environment orbitals, based on a mutual correlation criterion. The mutual correlation criterion makes eCAS systematically improvable without the need for any iteratively determined quantities.

item.title: Helper-assisted quantum sensing with low dressed-state leakage
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates that a dedicated “helper” qubit can imprint a transverse signal onto its phase while keeping the sensor qubit largely in its idle ground state, thereby reducing dressed‑state leakage and measurement back‑action—a long‑standing obstacle for high‑fidelity quantum metrology. By deriving an information bound under strict excitation budgets and showing how clever flip‑and‑sign reversal sequences can cancel static offsets with only modest (≈27 %) loss of Fisher information, the work builds on recent ancilla‑assisted readout schemes and offers a concrete pathway to more robust sensing in noisy solid‑state platforms. The results suggest that practical gains will hinge on device‑specific disturbance models, highlighting both the promise and the careful engineering required before helper‑only readout can outperform direct nondemolition verification.

We study a two-qubit sensing protocol in which only a helper qubit is read out. Calibrated loading and unloading encode a transverse signal in the helper's phase, keep leakage out of a selected dressed-state band small, and return the sensor close to its idle ground state. We derive an information bound for a single sensor whose excitation stays below a prescribed budget, and simulate repeated operation with an uncertain coupling and finite-duration resets in a driven open-system model. At the tested settings, finite measurement records support estimation with infrequent resets. A helper flip at zero coupling, combined with a reversal of the coupling sign, suppresses a static helper offset shared across a record while retaining the signal, at a cost of about 27% of the no-offset information of a plain sequence of equal duration. Under slowly varying noise, averaging each cycle's likelihood over the correct noise law removes most of the added bias, and a wrong noise law can worsen the estimate. A selected directly read sensor with ideal controls and repeated nondemolition verification has the higher information rate. Any practical benefit of avoiding direct readout therefore requires a device-specific disturbance model.

item.title: Entanglement diagnostics of stochastic-resetting steady states: theory and measurement on superconducting qubits
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that stochastic‑reset protocols can deliberately steer many‑body qubit arrays into exotic nonequilibrium steady states whose entanglement structure is tunable by the reset history—a capability that goes beyond what ordinary unitary dynamics can produce. By deriving closed‑form formulas for small Ising chains and confirming them on an IBM superconducting processor, the authors demonstrate that both entropy‑based and concurrence‑based diagnostics faithfully capture the predicted physics, while a simple depolarizing error model explains the modest loss of concurrence in real hardware. The work opens a practical route to using reset‑driven dynamics for quantum sensing of temporal information (via the Jensen gap/Holevo quantity) and for engineering robust entangled resources that could aid error mitigation or reservoir‑engineering schemes in near‑term devices.

Stochastic resetting drives quantum systems into nonequilibrium stationary states unreachable under uninterrupted unitary evolution, and their entanglement depends on whether the reset history is resolved or averaged over. We study this interplay in the transverse-field Ising chain, deriving closed-form results for two qubits and evaluating chains of up to 12 qubits exactly. In the two-qubit system, these closed-form results show that phase matching between energy eigenstates produces resonances, and their visibility in the stationary state is determined by the symmetry of the reset state. Measurements on an IBM superconducting processor show the entropies evaluated before and after the reset average closely following noiseless predictions with no fitted parameter, while concurrence lies below prediction across most of the hardware measurements. The two diagnostics respond differently because they read different components of the same reconstructed state, and a depolarizing model captures the concurrence suppression with one fitted parameter. The difference between the two entropies, i. e., the Jensen gap of entanglement entropy, equals the Holevo information that a subsystem retains about the time since the last reset. With a Bell-state reset, this information grows with chain length across a half-chain cut over the sizes studied, without visible saturation at the smaller reset probabilities. Since reset times are sampled and recorded classically, the trajectory-averaged entropy, and with it the Jensen gap, is obtained without postselection, in contrast to monitored circuits, where trajectory-resolved entanglement requires sampling exponentially rare measurement records.

item.title: Classical communication over quantum channels: does entanglement help in nature?
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article narrows the gap between theory and practice by showing that entangling codewords offers no boost for a broad family of physically relevant channels—including multi‑level amplitude‑damping, dephasing and other phase‑covariant maps—so many real‑world communication links are unlikely to benefit from exotic quantum tricks. It builds on Hastings’ breakthrough that disproved the “no‑advantage” conjecture but goes further by proving a Schur‑weighted block entropy inequality that rules out entanglement gains in low‑dimensional, experimentally accessible settings. For engineers designing quantum‑enhanced classical links, the result is reassuring: they can focus on optimizing conventional coding strategies without worrying about missing a hidden entanglement advantage.

Can entangling codewords across independent uses of a quantum channel improve the rate of classical communication? An old conjecture states that there is no such entanglement advantage for all channels. Although Hastings's result and follow-up works disproved this conjecture, it turns out that enormous dimension is required to construct a channel where entanglement enhances classical communication. This indicates that there might be no entanglement advantage for many physical channels, or for all low dimensional channels. Motivated by recent progress on (generalized) amplitude damping channels, we propose a general Schur-weighted block entropy inequality, and show that there is no entanglement advantage for all phase-covariant channels including multi-level amplitude damping channels, generalized dephasing channels, and damping-dephasing channels. As a by-product, we also recover the recently established result that there is no entanglement advantage for all qubit channels.

item.title: Algebraic strong-to-weak symmetry breaking and partial decodability in the surface code
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that even modest coherent Z‑rotations can drive the standard triangular‑lattice surface code into a new “partially decodable” critical regime, revealing universal scaling laws for decoding fidelity that depend only on the lattice aspect ratio. By mapping the problem to a replica SO(1) sigma model and confirming predictions with large‑scale simulations, the authors connect this behavior to an algebraic strong‑to‑weak symmetry‑breaking phase in a dual Z₂ paramagnet—an insight that bridges quantum error correction with concepts from statistical physics. The results suggest that realistic coherent noise may demand decoding strategies beyond conventional Pauli‑frame methods, highlighting both a fresh diagnostic tool for hardware engineers and a cautionary note for fault‑tolerance thresholds built on purely stochastic error models.

Coherent noise can give rise to unconventional regimes of quantum information recovery and mixed-state order. We study these phenomena in two settings related by Wegner duality: the triangular-lattice surface code subject to single-qubit Pauli-$Z$ rotations followed by syndrome measurements, and a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ paramagnet subject to strongly symmetric decoherence. Increasing the rotation angle drives a transition from a decodable phase to a \emph{partially decodable} critical phase in the code, and from a strongly symmetric phase to a phase with \emph{algebraic} $\mathbb{Z}_2$ strong-to-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking (SWSSB) in the dual paramagnet. We develop a common description of these phenomena in terms of a weakly coupled $\mathrm{SO}(n)$ nonlinear sigma model in the replica limit $n\to1$. Taking this replica limit analytically, we derive universal signatures of the critical phase: an optimal Pauli decoding fidelity that approaches a universal function of the system's aspect ratio in the thermodynamic limit, and a dual fidelity correlator that decays as a universal power law. These observables relate to correlations of twist operators in the sigma model description. Large-scale numerical simulations confirm these analytical predictions. We also argue that the algebraic SWSSB phase cannot be realized by any Pauli dephasing channel acting on the $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ paramagnet. We probe this "non-classical" character through the output state's sensitivity to well-separated $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ fluxes inserted in the initial state, which reveals persistent coherence between distinct $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ charge trajectories at long distances.

item.title: Grow, Compress, and Perturb: A Hybrid Quantum-Classical Pathway to Scalable Quantum Chemistry on Quantum Computers
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article introduces VULCAN, a gradient‑free, layered VQE framework that slashes the operator pool size by up to an order of magnitude and eliminates costly Hamiltonian‑gradient measurements, directly tackling one of the biggest bottlenecks in scalable quantum chemistry. By coupling a grow‑then‑compress ansatz construction with a stochastic Epstein‑Nesbet perturbative correction, the authors demonstrate chemical accuracy on systems as large as 32 logical qubits while using only a fraction of the measurement budget required by ADAPT‑VQE. If these techniques translate to near‑term hardware, they could accelerate the path toward practical quantum simulations of medium‑size molecules without prohibitive circuit depth or sampling overhead.

While Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) variants are among leading candidates for electronic structure calculations on quantum computers, gradient-based operator selection limits their scalability. To solve this, we introduce the Hamiltonian-gradient-free VULCAN (Variational Upbuilding, Layered Compression, Adaptive N-body perturbation) layered VQE framework. Our method dynamically generates ansatz operators using Variational Double Bracket Flow (VDBF) equations. Combined with a linearly scaling minimal complete pool, it creates a pool 4-12 times smaller than QEB (Qubit-Excitation-Based) pools. By appending entire layers simultaneously, Hamiltonian gradient measurements are completely eliminated. Circuit depth is managed via a grow-then-compress scheme using efficient state-overlap measurements, and qubit requirements are reduced by projecting the Hamiltonian onto a dominant-determinant subspace. Using high-performance emulation up to 32 logical qubits, we achieve chemical accuracy at just 5-20% of the measurement cost of batched ADAPT-VQE for hydrogen chains, BeH2 and H2O. For the 32-qubit C3H6, where batched ADAPT-VQE does not reach chemical accuracy, a single VULCAN layer combined with a GPU-accelerated stochastic Epstein-Nesbet (ENPT2) correction does. This stochastic ENPT2 post-processing step enables early termination at chemical accuracy.

item.title: Fast and accurate neural triage decoding of ultra-high-rate quantum LDPC codes
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article introduces a “neural triage” decoder that combines syndrome consistency checks with a lightweight neural message‑passing network, delivering near‑optimal error‑correction accuracy for ultra‑high‑rate qLDPC codes while cutting decoding latency by one to two orders of magnitude. The breakthrough matters because high‑rate qLDPC codes are among the most promising routes to dramatically reduce the physical qubit overhead required for fault‑tolerant quantum computers, yet their practical adoption has been hampered by slow, computationally intensive decoders. By showing that machine‑learning can be deployed adaptively—only invoking deeper neural processing when needed—the work bridges recent advances in neural belief‑propagation decoders with the real‑time demands of emerging quantum hardware. Readers should note that while the results are impressive for blocks of a few hundred logical qubits, scaling to larger distances and integrating the decoder into actual control stacks will be the next critical steps.

Quantum error correction is essential for fault-tolerant quantum computing. High-rate quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes have emerged as a promising approach to reducing the substantial physical qubit overhead of quantum error correction, enabling encoding rates exceeding $1/2$ in blocks of approximately one thousand physical data qubits. However, their practical implementation requires decoders that combine high accuracy with low latency to keep pace with quantum hardware. Existing decoders of high-rate qLDPC codes can achieve high accuracy but often incur substantial computational latency, whereas neural network decoders have yet to be demonstrated for high-rate qLDPC codes. Here, we introduce \emph{neural triage decoding}, a framework that uses syndrome consistency to adaptively allocate neural computation. A local neural message-passing network rapidly predicts error corrections, additional iterations reduce residual syndrome violations, and a rarely invoked diversification stage searches for consistent corrections to the remaining shots. We demonstrate that the \texttt{Triage} decoder can decode ultra-high-rate qLDPC codes encoding a few hundred logical qubits, including lifted-product and Kasai codes, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy comparable to the near optimal algorithmic decoders while reducing decoding latency by approximately one to two orders of magnitude. Our framework is inspired by a rigorous analysis of the exact bitwise marginal decoder, revealing a distance-independent syndrome-inconsistent error floor. In addition, we show the robustness of neural network decoders to mismatched error priors. Our results establish adaptive neural decoding as a promising route towards fast, accurate, and scalable quantum error correction in the near term.
